prompt: An Alpine image ends with `USER 10001:10001`, and its program fails with `touch: /data/report.txt: Permission denied`. `/data` was made earlier in the file by `RUN mkdir /data`. A colleague proposes `RUN mkdir /data && chmod 777 /data` as the fix. What is wrong with it?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 4; Docker and Containers, lesson 14.

choices.text: `chmod 777` is undone at once, since the umask that `mkdir` ran under strips the group's and others' write again
choices.why: A umask acts when a file is created. `chmod` is absolute and leaves exactly the mode it names.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: user 10001 needs `w` on `/data`, and 777 grants that permission just as well as a `chown` would
choices.why: Both let user 10001 write there. 777 also lets every other account in the container write there, and `chown` does not.

choices.text: Anyone in it could add or delete anybody's files there; `chown app:app /data` gives one user what it needs
choices.why: Creating and deleting are writes to the directory, so a world-writable one with no sticky bit makes everybody's files removable by anybody. The Docker course hands the directory to its user and nothing more.

choices.text: The denial came from a missing `x`, which 777 adds; under the default umask `mkdir` already let others create files
choices.why: Under the default umask `mkdir` gives root `rwxr-xr-x`. Others already have `x`; they lack `w`, and creating a file is a write to the directory.

prompt: A virtual machine built from a minimal image rebooted overnight, and the SOC asks for its ssh entries from before the reboot. `journalctl --list-boots` lists only the current boot, and `/var/log/journal` does not exist. What happened, and what stops the next reboot doing the same?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 5; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 2.

choices.text: It lived in `/run/log/journal`, in memory; creating `/var/log/journal` and restarting `systemd-journald` fixes it
choices.why: Without that directory journald keeps the journal on a tmpfs and loses it at every restart. Ubuntu creates the directory; minimal images often do not.

choices.text: `SystemMaxUse=` pushed the old boot out, and raising it in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` keeps more
choices.why: Rotation by size prunes a journal that is on disk. Here nothing was ever on disk, because the directory a persistent journal lives in is missing.

choices.text: An ordinary user sees their own entries and not the system's, and the same command under `sudo` lists the earlier boot
choices.why: Permission hides other people's messages, not whole boots. With no `/var/log/journal` there is nothing on disk for root to read either.

choices.text: A reboot that follows a crash throws the journal away on any machine, whatever its configuration says about keeping it
choices.why: `journalctl -b -1` is how you find out why a machine rebooted, which only works because a persistent journal outlives the reboot.

prompt: A pipeline stage is a bash script with `set -e` at the top, and its gate is one line: `trivy image --quiet --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 linkbox:dev | tee scan.txt`. The stage comes out green, and `scan.txt` lists four high findings, each with a fixed version. Why did the gate not stop it?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 6; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 8.

choices.text: `--exit-code 1` needs `--format json` to take effect, and this line prints the default table instead
choices.why: The pipeline course's own gate shows `--exit-code` deciding the verdict; the format changes what is printed, not the exit status.

choices.text: `--quiet` hides the exit status as well as the progress output, so the step passes whatever the scan finds
choices.why: `--quiet` only trims what is printed: the pipeline course's own gate runs with it and still exits 1 on a fixable high finding.

choices.text: `set -e` reacts when the first command of a pipeline fails, and in this line `trivy` is the one that comes first
choices.why: It is the other end: without `pipefail` a pipeline's status is its last command's, and every stage before it can fail silently.

choices.text: A pipeline's status is its last command's, and `tee` succeeded; `set -o pipefail` lets the scanner's 1 count
choices.why: `$?` after `trivy … | tee` is the 0 of `tee`, so `set -e` saw nothing wrong. With `pipefail`, or a look at `PIPESTATUS`, the gate fails as it should.

prompt: A Dockerfile's final stage installs a command-line tool written in C: a `RUN` line downloads its release binary with `curl` into `/usr/local/bin`. An advisory against that version came out last month, and Trivy's report on the image never mentions the tool. Why?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 7; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 8.

choices.text: Trivy leaves `/usr/local` alone, since that directory belongs to whoever runs the machine
choices.why: Trivy reads every list it finds, wherever it is. Here there is no list to find, because nothing recorded the tool.

choices.text: A scanner reads the records package managers keep, and nothing recorded this binary; `dpkg -S` cannot name it
choices.why: Installed outside every package manager, the tool is on no list, and a C program carries no record of its own. Installing it from a package, or writing it into the SBOM by hand, puts it on one.

choices.text: Trivy's database is downloaded once a day and holds the advisories of that day, not the older ones
choices.why: It is refreshed daily and merges advisories from all its sources; one published last month is in it.

choices.text: A binary that a `RUN` line brings in is scanned if an earlier stage of the same Dockerfile compiled it from source
choices.why: Where a binary was built does not matter. A Go binary carries its module record from anywhere; a C program carries none from anywhere.

prompt: A build server has collected software in six ways over two years. Which of these will `apt upgrade` never bring up to date? Choose all that apply.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 7.

choices.text: a release binary extracted into `/usr/local/bin`
choices.why: Nothing upgrades it and nothing removes it; `dpkg -S` cannot even say it is there.

choices.text: Docker, from `download.docker.com`, added with a key and a `signed-by` line
choices.why: A third-party repository is the good option because apt still manages it: `apt upgrade` upgrades Docker like anything else.

choices.text: a command-line tool installed with `pip install --user`
choices.why: A language package manager has its own registry and knows nothing of apt, and apt knows nothing of it.

choices.text: Firefox, installed on Ubuntu with `apt install firefox`
choices.why: On Ubuntu that command installs a snap, which has its own update mechanism; `apt list --installed` does not show it.

choices.text: a package from Ubuntu's `universe` component
choices.why: Maintained by the community, and still in a repository apt reads, so `apt upgrade` covers it.

choices.text: `python3-requests`, installed with `apt install`
choices.why: It is the distribution's own package, the first choice the lesson gives, and apt upgrades it with everything else.

prompt: Hunting through a web server's access log, an analyst stacks client addresses to read the rare end: `cut -d" " -f1 logs/access.log | uniq -c | sort -n | head`. The short tail is full of counts of 1 and 2, and `10.0.1.12` turns up on several of those lines. What went wrong?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 8; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 10.

choices.text: `sort -n` compared the counts as text rather than as numbers, so a `10` landed before a `9` and the order is wrong
choices.why: `-n` is what makes the sort numeric. Without it `100` would sort before `99`; with it the counts are in order.

choices.text: Field 1 is not the client's address in this log format; the address the analyst wanted sits in field 7 instead
choices.why: Field 1 is the address and field 7 is the path, which is why the lesson counts busy paths with `-f7`.

choices.text: Without a `sort` first, `uniq` counted runs of neighbouring lines, so a busy address split into small counts
choices.why: `uniq` collapses adjacent lines only. Unsorted, an address scattered through the log becomes dozens of tiny counts, and they fill exactly the end a hunt reads.

choices.text: The rare end also holds legitimate one-off visitors, and telling them apart from the rest is the validation step's job
choices.why: Rare legitimate visitors do sit there, but one of them would not repeat on several lines. That repetition comes from the pipeline, not the traffic.

prompt: A Windows build job reads its version with `Get-Content $versionFile -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`, so that the first build, before the file exists, does not stop. Months later somebody moves the file to another folder: the step carries on with an empty version, the job is green, and its log has no line about the file. Why is there no line?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 10.

choices.text: Cmdlet errors are terminating by default, so the moved file gave an empty read rather than any error at that point
choices.why: A cmdlet's errors are non-terminating by default: `Get-Content` reports `Cannot find path` and the script goes on.

choices.text: The error went into `$LASTEXITCODE`, and nothing in the job read it
choices.why: `$LASTEXITCODE` holds a native program's exit status. A cmdlet's failure shows in `$?` and in `$Error`.

choices.text: `SilentlyContinue` made the error non-terminating, whereas under the default `Continue` the whole job would have failed
choices.why: `Continue` reports the error and keeps going, so the job would still have been green, with the error printed in its log.

choices.text: `SilentlyContinue` neither reports nor stops, so it hides this missing file just as it hides the expected one
choices.why: It is lesson 8's `2>/dev/null` with the same flaw: it silences the error you expected and the one you did not.

prompt: On a database server, the on-call engineer reads `/proc/PID/oom_score` to see which process the kernel would pick first. One process has an `oom_score_adj` of 0 and uses half of the machine's memory. Building the score the way lesson 11 describes, about what should it read?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.

prompt: A worker keeps vanishing with exit status 137 and nothing in its own log. Put lesson 11's steps for it in order.
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.
items: Confirm it was memory, and not something else sending `KILL`
Run `dmesg -T | grep -i 'killed process'` for the process's name and the size it reached
Read whether the line says `Memory cgroup out of memory` or plain `Out of memory`
Ask whether its memory grew steadily or spiked, which only a graph over time answers
trap: The likeliest slip is changing a limit before reading the kernel's line. Until it says `Memory cgroup out of memory` or plain `Out of memory`, nobody knows whether a group's limit or the whole machine was reached.

prompt: So that the deploy account can change one setting, a pull request adds a rule under `/etc/sudoers.d/` letting it run `sudo vim /etc/nginx/nginx.conf` with no password. Its author calls the rule narrow, since it names one file. What should the reviewer answer?
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 12; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: The editor runs as root and `:!sh` inside it is a root shell; `sudoedit` edits as the user and installs as root
choices.why: A rule is narrow when what it allows is small, like a restart script and one `tail`. This one allows whatever a root editor can do, which is everything.

choices.text: It is narrow enough, as long as it goes in through `visudo -f`, which checks the rule first
choices.why: `visudo` checks a rule's syntax, not how much it grants; a correct line can still hand out root.

choices.text: `sudo` resets the environment on the way in, so the account's own vim configuration and plugins stay behind and do not run as root
choices.why: `env_reset` drops variables, and `sudo vim` still runs the editor as root with the user's configuration and plugins in it.

choices.text: The risk is `NOPASSWD`, and with a password prompt the same rule would be safe
choices.why: A password proves who is asking. It does not shrink what the rule lets them do once they have asked.

prompt: A sync job sometimes runs for ninety minutes, and there must always be a full hour of quiet between the end of one run and the start of the next. Complete the `[Timer]` line that counts from the moment its service last finished: `___=1h`
hint: Linux and the Command Line, lesson 13.

prompt: Ana committed `.env` with a live payment key, noticed at once, and ran `git reset --hard HEAD~1` before pushing anything. `git log` no longer shows the commit, and she asks whether anything else needs doing.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.

choices.text: It is settled: the key stayed on her laptop, and the hard reset took that commit off the branch for good
choices.why: The commit is on no branch, which is not the same as gone: her reflog keeps it for 30 days. And a key that reached a commit is treated as leaked whatever happened next.

choices.text: Revoke the key: the commit still sits in her reflog, and a key that reached a commit counts as leaked
choices.why: The reset only moved the branch. Rotating first is the one step that makes every copy worthless, the ones she knows about and the ones she does not.

choices.text: Reset back to the reflog entry, delete `.env` in a new commit, and push both
choices.why: That puts the key back on the branch and then publishes it. Deleting a file never changes the commit that added it.

choices.text: Push the branch so that the platform's scanner checks it, and then rewrite the history with `git filter-repo`
choices.why: Pushing makes copies on the server and in every fetch. Rewriting comes last, and the key keeps working throughout.

prompt: A team wants no secret and no unreviewed change to reach `main`, whoever pushes and from whatever machine. Which of these still hold for a developer who never set anything up on their own laptop? Choose all that apply.
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 8; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 6.

choices.text: protection on `main` at the hosting service: changes arrive only by an approved pull request
choices.why: None of it is Git: it lives on the server, which is why it binds everybody who pushes there and nobody who pushes elsewhere.

choices.text: a gitleaks `pre-commit` hook installed in each developer's own `.git/hooks` directory
choices.why: `.git/hooks` is not part of the repository, so a fresh clone has no hook, and `--no-verify` skips one that is there.

choices.text: a required pipeline stage that scans the whole history of every push for secrets
choices.why: Every push reaches the CI, so a secret that came in a merge, or from a laptop with no hook, is found there.

choices.text: a framework that installs the team's hooks from a file kept in the repository
choices.why: It solves how hooks reach each clone, and neither of the other gaps: `--no-verify`, and secrets that never pass through the hook.

choices.text: push protection on the platform, for the token formats the provider knows
choices.why: It runs on the server and refuses the push before it lands, whatever the laptop has. Its limit is the shapes it recognises.

choices.text: `.env` listed in the project's `.gitignore`
choices.why: It keeps one file out of `git add .`, which helps. A key pasted into the code, or a change nobody reviewed, passes it untouched.

prompt: A history scan reports a carrier token in a file that was deleted two commits later, so `git blame` has no line left to point at. Complete the command that lists every commit that added or removed the string: `git log ___ lab-live-token --oneline`
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 3; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.

prompt: A CI job checks out a project whose submodule address is a folder on the runner, and `git submodule update --init` is refused. Somebody proposes running `git config --global protocol.file.allow always` once on the runner, so nobody has to think about it again. Why does the Git course allow it per command, with `-c`, instead?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: Global settings are not read by Git on a CI runner, so a `-c` on the command itself is the way to reach the job
choices.why: A global setting applies to every Git command the runner's account runs, and that reach is exactly why it is too wide here.

choices.text: `-c` is needed for the first clone alone: after it the submodule is pinned and stops using the address
choices.why: The pin is a commit id. The address is still where the submodule is fetched from, which is why `.gitmodules` records it.

choices.text: Any repository it clones could aim a submodule at any folder on its disk; `-c` allows that once
choices.why: Set globally, every repository the runner ever clones could reach into its disk. With a real server's address the setting is not needed at all.

choices.text: The refusal is about speed, since a folder is copied file by file, and `-c` keeps that cost to one command
choices.why: The lesson's reason is safety: what a repository you clone could make Git read from your own disk.

prompt: Your team's library takes its version numbers from Conventional Commits. A commit that changes a response's format, so that callers have to adapt, goes in as `feat(api): return prices in cents`, with no `!` and no footer. A service that depends on the library has a bot that groups minor and patch updates into one pull request and merges it when the pipeline is green. What happens?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 11; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 18.

choices.text: The release tool refuses the commit, because a breaking `feat` is required to carry `BREAKING CHANGE:`
choices.why: The convention structures a message and cannot read its meaning. A `feat` with no `!` is taken as a feature that breaks nothing.

choices.text: The bot reads the library's commit messages and holds each `feat` back for a person instead of merging it on green
choices.why: A bot proposes versions, not commits. What decides grouping and merging here is whether the version is a major one.

choices.text: Nothing changes downstream, since bots order updates by release date and not by version number
choices.why: Grouping minor and patch updates while leaving majors alone is a decision made by version number.

choices.text: It counts as a new feature release, so it lands unattended once checks pass; a `!` would have made it a major, kept apart
choices.why: A major is the version allowed to break things, and that is why majors are kept apart. Without the `!` the break arrives labelled safe, and only the dependent's tests can stop it.

prompt: Release 2.4 came from `main` and broke checkout. The on-call engineer ran `rollback.sh`, and production was answering on 2.3 within two seconds. The commit that caused it, `7f3b2d1`, is on `main`, and everybody has pulled it. What belongs in the repository next?
hint: Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 4; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11.

choices.text: `git revert 7f3b2d1`, so `main` gains a commit that undoes it and everybody's copy of it still agrees
choices.why: Revert is the undo that is safe on a shared commit. Without it, the next release built from `main` ships the bug again.

choices.text: `git reset --hard` to the commit before it and a forced push, so `main` matches what production runs
choices.why: Rewriting a branch others have pulled leaves their copies disagreeing with yours, and forcing the push drops what they had.

choices.text: Nothing, since the rollback already undid the change and `main` can stay as it is
choices.why: The rollback swapped production's links and left the code where it was; the next release from `main` carries the bug.

choices.text: A revert, and from now on handle incidents by reverting and waiting for the pipeline instead of rolling back
choices.why: That is rolling forward to a new release. The default is to roll back in seconds first and then fix through the usual pipeline.

prompt: `deploy.sh` refuses any artifact whose SHA-256 differs from the `.sha256` file the build wrote beside it. Both files sit in a shared store that several people can write to. What does the check prove, and what would add what it cannot?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 7; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 14.

choices.text: That the artifact came out of the pipeline, since the build step is what writes the `.sha256` files
choices.why: Anybody who can write to the store can compute a hash and replace both files. A digest says which bytes, not who made them.

choices.text: That these are the bytes the hash names, catching a bad download or a stray edit; a signature by a key only the CI holds says who made them
choices.why: The check catches damage on the way. Saying who vouches for a digest takes a signature, and a signature is worth as much as the hold on its key.

choices.text: Little, because a SHA-256 value can be forged by whoever has the file; a longer hash would close that gap
choices.why: The bytes cannot change without the hash changing. The gap is that whoever replaces the file can write a new hash beside it.

choices.text: That the build was reproducible, and rebuilding from the tag inside the production job would prove the rest
choices.why: A rebuild is a new artifact that has never run anywhere, which is what building once and promoting the same bytes avoids.

prompt: A fix stops a patient from cancelling somebody else's booking, and its pull request adds one test. Which of these make that test worth keeping? Choose all that apply.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11; Secure Coding, lesson 19.

choices.text: it was run on the code before the fix and failed, then on the fix and passed
choices.why: Red on the bug and green on the fix is what shows it tests anything; a test never seen failing might not.

choices.text: it asserts the refusal, and that the other patient's booking is still booked
choices.why: Checking what was refused and that nothing changed catches a fix that answers with a refusal and cancels anyway.

choices.text: it brings the cancellation module to 100% line coverage
choices.why: Coverage says which lines ran, not which refusals were asked for, and a project can ship the flaw at high coverage.

choices.text: its name reads as the requirement it protects
choices.why: The name is what still explains the test once everybody who remembers the flaw has moved on.

choices.text: it checks the response's status code and nothing else
choices.why: A status code alone is the weak column: the booking could be cancelled behind a correct-looking answer.

choices.text: its commit message names the developer whose change let the flaw in
choices.why: A blameless account names what happened. Who wrote the line is not a cause anybody can act on.

prompt: A Brazilian shop's test suite needs identifiers that look real and belong to nobody. Match each one to what lesson 3 says the tests should use.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 3.

pairs.right: an address at `example.org`, `example.com` or `example.net`
a real CEP of a public place, such as `01310-100`
a number generated to pass the check digits
the numbers a payment provider publishes for its sandbox
the documentation range `192.0.2.0/24`, or one of its two siblings

right_distractors: a real customer's value with its last digits changed
an address copied from production's access log

prompt: The carrier lets an account hold two valid tokens for a while, and the team rotates shipquote's production token on a quiet Tuesday, with no leak behind it. Put the steps in order.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.
items: Create the new token while the old one keeps working
Deploy the new token to every place that uses it
Confirm from the logs that every consumer has switched
Revoke the old token
trap: Revoking before every consumer has switched is the outage the lab produced: the carrier answered `401` and the shop fell back to its table until production restarted with the new token.

prompt: Rows that testers created in staging turn up in the production database. Staging's configuration had one line copied from the wrong file. Which pair of habits does lesson 8 give against exactly this mistake?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 8.

choices.text: Staging works on a copy of production's data, so that a slip made there touches the copy rather than the original
choices.why: A copy of customers' data in staging is personal data under weaker controls, and it would not stop staging reaching the real database.

choices.text: Each environment reads one shared configuration file, so that no line can be copied from the wrong one
choices.why: Configuration differs per environment by design; the code is what stays the same.

choices.text: Staging is deployed by hand, so that somebody reads its configuration before each deploy
choices.why: Staging is the pipeline's, after the checks. A person handling the files is how a line gets copied from the wrong one.

choices.text: Only production's configuration holds its credentials, and its data services refuse other connections
choices.why: Either one alone stops the copied line from working: staging has no key to production, and production would not answer it.

prompt: A test fails about one run in ten with no change to the code, and the team is tired of pressing re-run. A colleague proposes that the pipeline retry failed tests once and count the second attempt as a pass. What does lesson 5 have the team do instead?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 5.

choices.text: Fix the random seed or the hash seed, so that the test gives exactly the same answer on every single run
choices.why: That freezes the accident the test passes by. The fix is to assert what the code promises, such as the set rather than its order.

choices.text: Keep the automatic retry, as long as it reruns just the test that failed and not the whole suite again
choices.why: A retried pass turns every flaky test green, including the one that was right to fail, however narrow the retry.

choices.text: Measure it in a loop, find the cause, and park it in a non-blocking job with an owner and a deadline
choices.why: That keeps the main run trustworthy without pretending the test is fine, and the loop says how flaky it really is.

choices.text: Delete the test, since one that fails one time in ten for no reason is measuring noise and not the code
choices.why: It may be catching a real dependence on time, order or randomness; quarantining it in the open keeps that question alive.

prompt: A fix makes a service refuse to cancel somebody else's booking, and review asks that each refusal also write one security event. The code logs through a `log` function it is handed, as shipquote's `price` does. Which test proves that line is written, and that nothing else is?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 2; Secure Coding, lesson 15.

choices.text: Pass `lines.append` as `log`, cause a refusal, and compare `lines` with a list holding exactly the expected line
choices.why: The list is a spy: it records what was logged, and comparing all of it catches a second, unexpected line as well.

choices.text: Pass a stub `log` that returns nothing, cause a refusal, and assert the refusal's return value
choices.why: A stub answers and records nothing, so the test cannot tell whether any line was written.

choices.text: Pass a plain `mock.Mock()` as `log`, cause a refusal, and check that the mock was called
choices.why: A plain `Mock` accepts any call, so it passes with the wrong text, or with a second line nobody expected.

choices.text: Pass `lines.append` as `log`, cause a refusal, and assert that `"refused" in lines[0]`
choices.why: That reads the first line only, so an extra line after it would pass unseen.

prompt: On a production machine, shipquote's carrier token can reach the program in four ways. Match each to who on that machine can read it there.
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.

pairs.right: every user on the machine

pairs.left: an argument such as `--carrier-token=` on the command line
pairs.right: anybody who lists the processes

pairs.left: an environment variable set by whatever starts the process
pairs.right: the process's owner and root
only the account that owns the file

right_distractors: the members of the file's group, and nobody else
nobody, once the CI service masks it

prompt: A team sets its objective at 99.95% over 30 days, for a service that is either up or down. Working as lesson 11's table does, how many minutes of down time does that budget allow?
hint: Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 11.

prompt: Trivy flags a library in the staff portal's image with `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:N`, score 8.2. The portal is reachable only from the office network, and every sign-in needs a second factor. Of the four questions lesson 2 says move likelihood, which does that vector answer for the shop?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 2; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 5.

choices.text: Each of them, because `AV:N` already records that the portal faces the internet
choices.why: `AV:N` says the flaw can be exploited over a network at all. Who can reach this copy of it is a fact about the shop, and the base score assumes the worst.

choices.text: Motivation, since a score in the high band means scanners are sweeping for the flaw
choices.why: Whether anybody is trying is what EPSS estimates and KEV records. CVSS says how bad it would be, not whether anyone is looking.

choices.text: Ease alone; exposure and the controls already in the way are the shop's to answer
choices.why: No conditions, no account and no click describe how hard the flaw is to use. The base score assumes the code is reached and exposed, so reachability and MFA are yours to weigh.

choices.text: The damage side instead: a vector rates confidentiality, integrity and availability
choices.why: The last three fields do. `AV`, `AC`, `PR` and `UI` come first, and they describe what exploiting the flaw takes.

prompt: The owners gave the public website an RTO of 2 hours, and lesson 1 put 99.9% availability at about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month. Suppose the site goes down once in a 30-day month and is selling again exactly when its RTO runs out. What availability did it reach that month, in percent?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lessons 1 and 12.

prompt: The shop's API now runs in a cluster. The team applies a `deny-all` NetworkPolicy to the `shop` namespace and then one small policy per path, such as `allow-front`, which lets pods labelled `app: front` reach the shop's pods on port 8080. In a review they call the cluster Zero Trust. What does lesson 7 say they have built?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 7; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 24.

choices.text: Microsegmentation, its network half; no request is yet judged on who is asking
choices.why: Each workload has a boundary and each connection is allowed explicitly. What decides access is still which pod the packet came from, so a compromised `front` pod gets everything the shop answers.

choices.text: The whole of it, because each connection between two pods is now allowed by name
choices.why: Allowing paths explicitly is where Zero Trust's network side ends. The principles also ask for identity, device and context on every request, which a pod label is not.

choices.text: A perimeter, not Zero Trust: network policies are lesson 5's edge moved inside, which Zero Trust replaces
choices.why: Zero Trust does not take the segments away; it adds a decision in front of each resource. Microsegmentation is one of the ideas it is built from.

choices.text: Trust by location again, so the policies should go and identity checks replace them
choices.why: A label does stand in for a location, but the lesson keeps the network layers. The fix is to add the per-request decision, not to remove a layer that limits a compromised pod.

prompt: A review counts the layers between the internet and the production database of a small team's service. Which of these pairs are one layer drawn twice? Choose all that apply.
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 4.

choices.text: The CI deploy token and the database's administrator password are the same string, in one CI variable
choices.why: One secret behind two controls: whoever reads that variable passes both, so one leak opens both.

choices.text: The engineer who writes the production firewall rules is also the one person who approves them
choices.why: One person on both sides of the check: one mistake, or one stolen account, passes the rule and its review together.

choices.text: Two web application firewalls in a row, from one vendor, running the same version
choices.why: One bug in that version opens both. The lesson's case for two firewalls is two vendors, which fail for different reasons.

choices.text: A sign-in in front of the API, then a file permission that keeps the API's account out of the payroll
choices.why: The password and the operating system's permissions fail for different reasons. In the lab a leaked password got past the first and touched the second not at all.

choices.text: A sign-in that refuses wrong passwords, and a log that records each request whatever the answer
choices.why: The log relies on nothing the sign-in relies on. It recorded the leaked password's misuse when every preventive layer had held.

choices.text: An outer firewall and an inner one from different vendors, either side of the public servers
choices.why: That is the two-firewall DMZ the lessons describe as two layers, precisely because the vendors differ.

prompt: The shop moves to a cloud network. Its web servers sit in a subnet whose route table sends `0.0.0.0/0` to the internet gateway; the orders database sits in a subnet whose own table holds only `local`. To speed up product pages, a developer proposes a read-only copy of the orders database inside the web servers' subnet, with a security group that admits only the web servers. What is wrong with it, in lesson 5's terms?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 5; Cloud Security, lesson 8.

choices.text: It is fine, since the copy has no public address and a route alone is half of exposure
choices.why: True of reaching the copy from the internet. The web server the internet reaches is the client the security group admits, and once it is compromised it reads the whole copy.

choices.text: It puts the data in the zone the internet reaches, which should ask for it through one port and not keep a copy
choices.why: A public zone asks the inside for what it needs and holds no copy, so a compromised web server can do only what it was allowed. A copy beside it hands over everything at once.

choices.text: A subnet with no table of its own follows the main table, so the copy would sit in a private subnet anyway
choices.why: That is how the records subnet stayed private. This subnet has a table of its own, and that table leads to the internet gateway.

choices.text: A read-only copy skips encryption at rest, so a stolen snapshot would expose the orders
choices.why: Nothing in either course says so. The objection is where the data sits, beside the most exposed machine, not how it is stored.

prompt: The staff portal moves into a container that must listen on port 80. Its image has no `USER` line, so the program runs as root. Which way of starting it gives the container what lesson 6's portal had on the bare server, and nothing more?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 6; Docker and Containers, lesson 21.

choices.text: `--privileged`, which is how Docker grants a port below 1024
choices.why: It hands over every capability the daemon holds and the host's devices, and switches AppArmor and seccomp off: the opposite of one piece of root's power.

choices.text: `--cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE`
choices.why: Root's power is split into capabilities, and the portal needed exactly one: the right to listen on a low port. Drop every one and add that one back.

choices.text: No flags, since root inside a container starts with zero capabilities until it is given some
choices.why: A root process in a container holds 14 by default, among them changing file owners and switching users. Docker chose them so that most images work, not as a minimum.

choices.text: `--read-only`, because a root unable to write a file is a root unable to do harm
choices.why: A read-only filesystem stops writes to the image. The process keeps its 14 capabilities and can still kill, `chown` a mounted file or open raw sockets.

prompt: A pull request adds `/invoices/<id>` to the staff portal. A signed-in member of staff asking for somebody else's invoice gets `403`, and asking for an id that does not exist gets `404`. One reviewer wants it to refuse non-owners before it looks the invoice up, as the payslip code does; another wants `404` for both, as the exam portal in the secure coding course does. Who is right?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 8; Secure Coding, lesson 13.

choices.text: The second: a `403` reveals that the record exists, so it is the unsafe answer
choices.why: The payslip code answers `403` before it checks existence, so ana got the same `403` for carla, who does not exist, as for bruno. A `403` says nothing when it comes before the lookup.

choices.text: The first: a `404` for an invoice that exists is false, and status codes should stay true
choices.why: The secure coding lesson chooses `404` on purpose, and keeps `403` for places where existence is no secret and the person needs to know they lack permission.

choices.text: Neither: the endpoint should answer `200` with an empty body, so that the request leaves no trace in the answer
choices.why: An empty success hides the refusal from the person and from the log, where a run of refusals from one session is the signal worth an alert.

choices.text: Both: either way a non-owner gets the same answer whether or not the invoice exists
choices.why: The leak is two answers telling existing ids from missing ones. Refusing before the lookup and answering `404` to both each remove the difference, which is what both lessons protect.

prompt: The team measures its secret scanner the way lesson 11 measured the sign-in detector. Match each result of `gitleaks` in the pipeline to its outcome.
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 11; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 6.

pairs.left: it exits 1 on the administration token written into the settings file
pairs.right: true positive

pairs.left: it exits 1 on `a-token-for-the-tests-only`, which opens nothing anywhere
pairs.right: false positive

pairs.left: it exits 0 while a real key sits on a branch that exists only in a colleague's clone
pairs.right: false negative

pairs.left: it exits 0 on a commit that holds no credential at all
pairs.right: true negative

right_distractors: precision
recall

prompt: At a threshold of 3, the shop's sign-in rule raises 21 alerts a week, and seven of its false positives come from `svc-backup`, whose password expired, failing every night. Which change does lesson 11 prefer?
hint: Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 11; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 6.

choices.text: Give the backup job a working credential, so its failures stop at the source
choices.why: With the cause gone the rule needs no exception, and the night the backup account fails six times again is news worth an alert.

choices.text: Leave `svc-backup` out by name: precision rises to 64% and recall stays at 82%
choices.why: The numbers are right and the change is not free. An exception by name is a hole by name: anyone who learns it can guess against that account in silence.

choices.text: Lower the rule's severity to low, so the nightly alerts stop waking anybody
choices.why: Severity says what an alert means if it is true. Lowering it because the rule is noisy hides the problem in the one field meant to show it.

choices.text: Go back to a threshold of 5, where the backup job's seven windows were the false ones
choices.why: At 5 the slow guesser sails under the rule and recall falls to 27%: fewer alerts bought by missing most of the exercise.

prompt: The clinic's sign-in answers `wrong password` both for an address with no account and for a wrong password. A tester notices that a missing account is refused at once, while a real one takes the quarter of a second Argon2id costs. What does lesson 5 do about it?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 5; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 8.

choices.text: Compare the computed hash with the stored one in constant time
choices.why: That hides how much of one value matched another. Here no hash is computed at all for a missing account, so there is nothing for the comparison to hide.

choices.text: Lower the Argon2id cost until a real account answers as fast as a missing one
choices.why: A missing account still costs nothing, so the gap only shrinks. And every guess against a leaked store gets cheaper by the same factor.

choices.text: Verify against a fixed decoy hash when the requested account does not exist
choices.why: Both paths then pay for one Argon2id computation, so the time says no more than the words. A refusal should not answer a question nobody was allowed to ask.

choices.text: Say `no such user` honestly, since the timing already gives the answer away
choices.why: On a clinic's portal, whether an address has an account is a fact about somebody's health. The fix closes the second channel rather than opening the first.

prompt: Ana signs in with the right password, and her stored line is `$argon2id$v=19$m=7168,t=1,p=1$…`, below the policy of `m=19456,t=2`. Put what the application does in order, as lesson 5 describes it.
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 5.
items: Read the algorithm, the cost and the salt written in Ana's stored line
Recompute from what she typed with those parameters, and compare in constant time
Notice that the stored parameters are below the policy
Hash the same password again with the policy's parameters and a fresh salt
Replace the stored line while the password is still in memory
trap: Verifying with the policy's parameters instead of the stored ones would refuse every old hash, and rehashing before the comparison would store a hash of whatever was typed, right or wrong.

prompt: To keep the database password out of the configuration, a team seals it with AES-GCM into `db-password.gcm`. Their Dockerfile copies the sealed file and `aes-256.hex` into the image, opens the password at build time, and deletes `aes-256.hex` in a later `RUN`. The finished image has no key file in it. How should a reviewer classify the password's protection?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 11; Docker and Containers, lesson 14.

choices.text: Encryption, because the key is no longer anywhere in the image's filesystem
choices.why: It is gone from the merged view only. A later layer adds a whiteout; the layer below still holds the file, and every pull downloads it.

choices.text: Encoding, because the sealed file is stored as Base64 like any other ciphertext
choices.why: Base64 is how bytes travel as text. What decides the category is the key, and here there is one.

choices.text: Encryption, provided nobody runs `docker history` on the image
choices.why: Hiding how the image was built is not a key kept apart. Anybody who pulls the image has both halves whether they look or not.

choices.text: Obfuscation, because the key ships inside the image with the data it protects
choices.why: The test is who holds the key. A key that travels with the data, here in an earlier layer, makes it obfuscation with better mathematics.

prompt: The clinic's `portal-db` Secret holds the database password under `data:` as `Vi1kYi1zM2NyZXQtMjAyNg==`. Which of these protect that password? Choose all that apply.
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 11; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 14.

choices.text: RBAC rules that limit who is allowed to `get` Secrets in that namespace
choices.why: Anybody who can read the object through the API gets the password, so who may read it is the first protection.

choices.text: The API server encrypting Secrets before it writes them to etcd, with a key it is given
choices.why: That protects a copy of etcd's data that leaks. Through the API the server still decrypts for whoever is allowed.

choices.text: Keeping the manifest out of the Git repository
choices.why: A Secret manifest in Git, Base64 and all, is a password in Git.

choices.text: The Base64 under `data:`, which turns the password into unreadable text
choices.why: Base64 is an encoding: `base64 -d` gives the password back with no key.

choices.text: Applying ROT13 before the Base64, as the scheduler's vendor does
choices.why: That is obfuscation, two commands and no key, and every installation shares the trick.

choices.text: Declaring the Secret `type: Opaque` rather than leaving the type out
choices.why: The type says what shape the data has. It hides nothing and protects nothing.

prompt: The SOC holds a capture of last week's TLS 1.3 sessions between customers and the shop's web server. Operations hand over the private key of the server's certificate so the analysts can read the requests. What does that key give them?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 7; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 18.

choices.text: Each recorded session's content, since the certificate's key protected its session key
choices.why: That was RSA key transport, which TLS 1.3 removed. Each session's keys came from a fresh exchange whose private halves were discarded.

choices.text: No help with the content, because in TLS 1.3 the certificate's key just signs each handshake
choices.why: In TLS 1.3 the long-term key proves identity and never encrypts a session key. The analysts still have the addresses, ports, times, sizes and the server name.

choices.text: The sessions recorded after the key was exported, from that moment on
choices.why: No moment changes that: the exchange that made each session's keys never used the certificate's key. Whoever holds it can impersonate the server to new visitors, which is another matter.

choices.text: The certificate and the server name, which TLS 1.3 encrypts under the server's key
choices.why: The server name travels in the clear in the ClientHello, and the certificate is encrypted with handshake keys from the exchange, not with the server's key.

prompt: After the restore that rewound its counter, the agenda export starts recording each sealed file's nonce in a column of its own. So that a repeated nonce is refused at the moment of the second insert, instead of being found later by an audit, that column gets a unique ___.
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 17.

prompt: Vereda's CI checks that every commit carries a good SSH signature, verifying it against `allowed_signers` as found in the pull request's own checkout. A contributor's pull request adds a line to that file with a key of their own and a commit signed with it, and CI reports the signature good. What is wrong?
hint: Applied Cryptography, lesson 6; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 14.

choices.text: The file is the trust decision, and the pull request rewrote it; the verifier should read it from the protected branch
choices.why: Whoever controls the list of signers decides whose keys count. Read from the pull request, the list was chosen by the person being checked, like a public key pushed beside the image it verifies.

choices.text: It is fine, because an Ed25519 signature is unforgeable without its private key
choices.why: Nothing was forged. The signature is genuine, made by a key the contributor added to the list that was supposed to judge it.

choices.text: CI should compare each commit's SHA-256 digest with the one recorded in the pull request
choices.why: A digest has no key: whoever can change the commit can change its digest too. It says nothing about who made it.

choices.text: A shared HMAC key would have stopped it, since contributors do not hold that key
choices.why: Every verifier of an HMAC can also produce one, so CI would hold the power to sign. A signature exists to keep signing and checking apart.

prompt: With Calico running, the team applies `deny-all` to the `shop` namespace. Then `wget -T 3 shop.shop` from `stranger`, in another namespace, prints `download timed out`, and so does `wget -T 3 shop` from `front`, inside `shop`. A teammate concludes the shop's pods have crashed, since a policy would answer at once with a refusal. What do the two timeouts say?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 3; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 24.

choices.text: The teammate is right, because `front` sits in the protected namespace and a policy leaves its own neighbours alone
choices.why: Deny-all means all: `podSelector: {}` selects every pod in the namespace, and no rule admits `front` until one is added.

choices.text: The plugin is ignoring the policy, because an enforced policy would make `wget` fail with an error at once
choices.why: An ignored policy lets the answer through, as kindnet did on the first cluster. A failure is what enforcement looks like here.

choices.text: The attempts were discarded silently on the way, which is what a drop looks like; deny-all covers `front` too
choices.why: A refusal comes back at once from a machine where nothing listens. Silence until the timeout is something in between discarding the attempt, here the policy, on every pod in the namespace.

choices.text: The name `shop.shop` no longer resolves, because the policy also blocks the cluster's DNS
choices.why: The policy has `policyTypes: [Ingress]` on the shop's pods; it says nothing about traffic leaving `stranger`, and a name that failed would say so rather than time out on the download.

prompt: The shop's firewall runs the zone rules of the security course: the office cannot reach `db:5432`, and `www` may. A developer in the office who can SSH into `www` runs `ssh -f -N -L 5432:192.168.20.30:5432 www` and then queries the database through `127.0.0.1:5432` on the laptop. What happened, and what refuses it?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 7; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 5.

choices.text: The firewall dropped it, since the office may not reach the servers whatever program asks
choices.why: The firewall never saw the office talking to the database. It saw SSH to `www`, which rule 3 allows, and `www` to `db:5432`, which rule 2 allows.

choices.text: It works because SSH listens on 22; moving `www`'s SSH to another port closes it
choices.why: A different port hides nothing and changes nothing about what sshd forwards once a connection is in.

choices.text: SSH hid the traffic from the firewall by encrypting it; a firewall able to decrypt SSH is what it takes to stop it
choices.why: Encryption is not what got it through. The rules judge addresses and ports, and both legs of the tunnel are legs the rules allow.

choices.text: `www` made the last leg, which rule 2 allows; `AllowTcpForwarding no` on `www` refuses it
choices.why: The destination of `-L` is reached from the server's side, so the laptop borrowed `www`'s right to reach the database. A server that must not carry tunnels says so in its own configuration.

prompt: From home, Ana runs `ssh -J ana@office.example.com:2222 www.example.com`. `www` accepts SSH only from the office's public address. Put what happens in order, as lesson 7 describes it.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 7.
items: ssh signs Ana in to the office server, through the router's port 2222
The office server opens a connection to `www.example.com` port 22, which www's firewall admits
Home and www agree keys through that connection, and home checks www's host key in its own `known_hosts`
www accepts the key Ana's agent offers from home
trap: The office server checks nothing about www: it only relays bytes. The host key is checked at home, after the relay is open, which is why home's `known_hosts` gained www's key.

prompt: Ana's server once refused a forged `Invoice overdue` with `550 5.7.1 rejected by DMARC policy for example.net`. Today a message asking finance to pay a supplier's invoice into a new account arrives from the supplier's real address, sent through the supplier's own server after one of their passwords was stolen. Its headers show `spf=pass`, `dkim=pass` and `dmarc=pass`. What stops the payment?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 9; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 6.

choices.text: Publishing `p=reject` for the shop's own domain, so that forged mail is refused
choices.why: The shop's DMARC record rules mail that claims to come from the shop. This message claims the supplier, and the supplier's own server sent it.

choices.text: A second person calls the supplier, on a number already on record, before money moves
choices.why: DMARC proves the supplier's server sent the message, which is true. Whether the supplier meant it is a question only a channel the sender did not choose can answer.

choices.text: The check that already ran: DMARC refuses a message that asks for money to go to a new account
choices.why: DMARC reads which domain proved itself, not what the message asks. Every check passed because every check was honestly met.

choices.text: Reading the `Received:` lines bottom up to be sure the supplier's server sent it
choices.why: They will show exactly that. The supplier's server did send it, which is the problem rather than the answer.

prompt: A user forwards an order email to the SOC as suspicious, and its source carries the lines below. Match each to what it establishes.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 9.

pairs.right: the connecting server may send for the envelope sender's domain
example.com's key signed the named headers and the body, unchanged since
a pass held for the same domain as the From: line a person reads
the envelope sender the message was handed over with

right_distractors: the sender's mail program encrypted the message end to end
the sending address has a reverse name under in-addr.arpa

prompt: The shop moves its staff portal to the cloud and keeps lesson 11's rule: an alert when one address fails to sign in at least 3 times within ten minutes. All nine staff reach it from the office, whose router masquerades every laptop as `203.0.113.2`. What does that do to the rule?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 2; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 11.

choices.text: The nine become one address: their slips add up, and a block shuts out the office
choices.why: The portal sees the router's address for every laptop. Three staff each mistyping once in ten minutes now look like one source failing three times, and a block by address locks out all nine.

choices.text: Little, because the portal's log still records each laptop's `192.168.10.x` address
choices.why: The router rewrites the source on the way out and puts it back only on replies. Outside, every laptop is `203.0.113.2`.

choices.text: It removes the false positives, since failures from the office's own address can be trusted
choices.why: That is trust by location. An infected office laptop guessing passwords also arrives as `203.0.113.2`.

choices.text: It raises recall, because a guesser in the office can no longer spread failures over several addresses
choices.why: The guesser was never in the office. What changes is that harmless failures from nine people now share one count, which is the false positive side.

prompt: Ana added `PasswordAuthentication no` at the end of `/etc/ssh/sshd_config` and reloaded sshd. The audit wants evidence that the server really refuses passwords. Which of these are that evidence? Choose all that apply.
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 7; Information Security Fundamentals, lesson 16.

choices.text: `sshd -T` printing `passwordauthentication no`
choices.why: It prints the settings sshd really uses, after every file it reads, which is the only reading that settles it.

choices.text: A client told not to offer a key being refused with `Permission denied (publickey).`
choices.why: Told not to offer a key, the client is refused, and the refusal names what is still allowed: only `publickey`.

choices.text: `grep PasswordAuthentication /etc/ssh/sshd_config` showing the line she appended
choices.why: sshd keeps the first value it reads, and Ubuntu reads `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf` first. A `yes` there wins while the main file looks right.

choices.text: `sshd -t` exiting 0 after the change
choices.why: Lower-case `t` checks that the configuration parses, so a mistake does not lock everybody out. It says nothing about which value won.

choices.text: The comment `#PasswordAuthentication yes` still sitting higher up in the file
choices.why: A commented line is not a setting at all; the default and every included file decide, which is why the checklist reads `sshd -T`.

prompt: The SOC has `/tmp/web.pcap` from the laptop and wants only the packets that open or end each connection, the handshake and the goodbye. Complete the filter: `tcpdump -n -r /tmp/web.pcap "tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-___) != 0"`
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 10.

prompt: A deploy step should fail when the certificate the server actually sends has less than two weeks left. It reads that certificate with `openssl s_client` and pipes it into `openssl x509 -noout -checkend N`. What should N be?
hint: Networks and Protocols, lesson 6.

prompt: linkbox's `ci/sast.sh` begins with `set -euo pipefail`, runs Semgrep with `--error`, then Bandit with `--severity-level medium`. Run 1 failed in `sast` on Semgrep's two findings. The developer fixes exactly those two and pushes, and run 2 fails in `sast` again, on Bandit's B201 for the debugger. She says the scanner missed it the first time. What happened?
hint: Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 3.

choices.text: Bandit reports once Semgrep has passed, because the two tools share one set of rules
choices.why: They share nothing: Bandit's checks are its own. It simply never started in run 1.

choices.text: B201 is high severity, and the gate reads high findings after the medium ones are fixed
choices.why: `--severity-level medium` reports medium and high together, in one run; the threshold is a floor, not an order of reading.

choices.text: `set -e` stopped the script at Semgrep's failure, so Bandit did not run in run 1
choices.why: A stage that stops at its first tool reports only that tool's findings. B201 was in the code all along, and it appears once Semgrep's are fixed.

choices.text: Fixing the search moved the line numbers, and Bandit reports a moved line as a new finding
choices.why: Bandit keeps no memory between runs; it would have reported B201 in run 1 had it run at all.

prompt: A monthly security report quotes `pip-audit -r requirements.txt` on the portal's old lock, which printed `Found 12 known vulnerabilities in 2 packages`. The rows for jinja2 3.1.4 name `PYSEC-2026-1475`, `PYSEC-2026-1472`, `PYSEC-2026-1471`, `PYSEC-2026-1471`, `PYSEC-2026-1475` and `PYSEC-2026-1472`; the rows for requests 2.31.0 name `PYSEC-2026-1873`, `PYSEC-2026-1872`, `PYSEC-2026-2275`, `PYSEC-2026-1873`, `PYSEC-2026-1872` and `PYSEC-2026-2275`. Counting the way the pipeline course asks before a number goes into a report, how many flaws should the report state?
hint: Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 5; Secure Coding, lesson 17.

prompt: linkbox's `ci/exceptions.txt` holds three lines excepting Jinja2 3.1.4's advisories until `2026-11-20`, with reasons such as `templates need rework for 3.1.5; Ana, see issue 41`. In the last week the gate starts warning, and a teammate runs `sed` to change all three dates to `2027-01-20`, keeps the reason, and commits it as "bump dates". The build is green again. What do the two courses find wrong with that commit?
hint: Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 7; Threat Modelling and Risk, lesson 12.

choices.text: A renewal is a new decision: the risk reviewed, and a reason saying what changed
choices.why: Both courses refuse the moved date. An exception that renews itself by an edit becomes the permanent acceptance its date was there to prevent.

choices.text: The gate reads the date, so a later date that a reviewer lets through is a valid renewal
choices.why: The gate checks the date because a program can. Whether the decision still holds is what the reason and the review are for, and this commit carries neither.

choices.text: Each line should name the package instead of one advisory, so a single date covers the next advisory too
choices.why: Naming the advisory is deliberate: a fourth advisory against 3.1.4 is not covered, and it breaks the build like any other.

choices.text: Exceptions are not renewable; the build has to stay broken until Jinja2 is upgraded
choices.why: Both courses allow a renewal. What they refuse is one made by moving a date with no new decision behind it.

prompt: A team ships two programs in one image. The build stage compiles a Go service with `CGO_ENABLED=0` and a small C tool linked against a compression library somebody copied into the repository; the final stage is `gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12` and receives both binaries with `COPY --from=build`. The image scan reports very little. Which part of what ships has no list the scanner can read?
hint: Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 8; Docker and Containers, lesson 13.

choices.text: The Go service: a static binary on a base with no package manager leaves the scanner no record
choices.why: Go records its module dependencies inside the binary, and Trivy reads that record, static or not.

choices.text: Neither: distroless records the copied binaries in the Debian package database too
choices.why: That database lists the base's own packages. Files the build stage copies in are on no list unless something writes one.

choices.text: Both binaries: the scanner reads a program's bytes, and a compiled binary hides what went into it
choices.why: A scanner does not recognise code from its bytes. It reads the records package managers, and some compilers, leave behind.

choices.text: The C tool and its library: nothing recorded them, so the report is silent about them
choices.why: A C program compiled in the build records nothing. The way out is to write the component into the SBOM by hand: a clean report is a statement about the lists.

prompt: A Deployment runs an image whose Dockerfile ends with `USER 65532`, and its container sets `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` and `capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}`. To get past a permission error, somebody adds `runAsUser: 0` to the container in a hurry, and the pod starts as root. Which one field, had it been there, would have turned that edit into a refusal?
hint: Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 9; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 25.

choices.text: `seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}`, since a root process makes calls the filter refuses
choices.why: The filter limits which system calls a process may make, whoever it runs as. It says nothing about the user.

choices.text: `runAsNonRoot: true`: the kubelet then refuses to start a container whose user would be 0
choices.why: It is the one control that checks the user: the pod waits in `CreateContainerConfigError` instead of running. `USER` in the image is only what happens when nothing says otherwise.

choices.text: `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` on the pod as well, since root fails to start on a read-only root
choices.why: It was already set, and it still held: root cannot change the image's files. Nothing about a read-only root stops root from starting.

choices.text: `capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}` moved to the pod, so that root has no capability left to use
choices.why: Root without capabilities still starts. Dropping them limits what root can do, not whether it runs.

The job can ask for that token only when its workflow grants the permission `id-token: ___`.
hint: Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 14; Automated Testing and CI/CD, lesson 9.

hint: Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 16.

the title handed to the step under `env:` and read as `$TITLE`
