the API server's own `/metrics`

prompt: The pipeline's ServiceAccount `deployer` is bound in `shop` to lesson 23's Role: `get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update` and `patch` on `deployments` in `apps`, and `get`, `list` and `watch` on `pods` and `pods/log`. Which of these will it be allowed to do? Choose all that apply.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 23.

choices.text: Change the image of the `shop` Deployment in `shop`
choices.why: That is an update or a patch of a Deployment in the Role's namespace, which is what the Role exists for: rolling out a new version.

choices.text: Read the logs of a shop pod in `shop`
choices.why: `pods/log` is named in the Role. Had it been left out, reading the pods would not have included their logs.

choices.text: List the pods in `shop`
choices.why: `list` on `pods` is granted, and the namespace is the binding's own.

choices.text: Delete the `shop` Deployment
choices.why: `delete` is not among the verbs, on purpose: the lesson's capture shows the refusal, `cannot delete resource "deployments"`.

choices.text: Open a shell in a shop pod with `kubectl exec`
choices.why: `pods/exec` is a subresource nobody named, so `create pods/exec` answers `no` although reading the pod is allowed.

choices.text: List the pods in `default`
choices.why: A RoleBinding grants only inside its own namespace, and this one lives in `shop`.

prompt: One shop pod has been making connections nobody can explain. The on-call engineer wants to run `kubectl delete pod` at once, since the Deployment will start a clean one. The cluster runs no log collector. By the SOC course's rule for containment, what does deleting it first throw away?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 41; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 13.

choices.text: Nothing: `kubectl logs --previous` still reads the deleted pod's output
choices.why: `--previous` reads the container before the last restart, in the same pod. A deleted pod has no previous container to read.

choices.text: Nothing lasting: the pod's events keep the same lines for an hour afterwards
choices.why: Events are what the scheduler and the kubelet said about the pod, not what the process wrote. They expire after an hour anyway.

choices.text: What its process printed: the node deletes that log file with the pod
choices.why: `kubectl logs` reads a file under `/var/log/pods`, and the file goes when the pod does. Collect, then act: copy the logs, and the open connections, before the pod is removed.

choices.text: Its image, which the node removes from its own disk together with the pod
choices.why: The image stays on the node and in the registry. What goes is the record of what this particular process did.

prompt: A container of the shop Deployment declares `limits: cpu: 250m`. On its node, the container's control group shows how much processor time it may have in each period of 100,000 microseconds. Complete what `cpu.max` reads: `___ 100000`.
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 19; Linux and the Command Line, lesson 11.

prompt: A Deployment runs 8 replicas, and its `strategy.rollingUpdate` was never written, so both fields keep their default. A new image crashes on start, and the rollout stalls. Reasoning as lesson 35 does about its four-replica shop, how many pods of the old version are still serving?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 35.

prompt: A team weighs running its own control plane against a managed one at 0.10 dollars an hour. Its own would need the three machines lesson 46 counts for etcd, at 0.05 dollars an hour each, and about 4 hours of an engineer's time a month at 50 dollars an hour. The cluster also has six worker nodes at 0.20 dollars an hour each. In lesson 46's sum, with a month of 730 hours, what does running the control plane yourself cost per month, in dollars?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 46.

prompt: The pod `crashing` exits the moment it starts, and its image holds one program and no shell. You want to see the environment it was started with, and keep the broken pod exactly as it is, as evidence. Which command does that?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 42.

choices.text: `kubectl exec crashing -- env`
choices.why: There is no running container to enter, and the image has no `env` program to run if there were.

choices.text: `kubectl debug crashing --copy-to=crashing-debug --container=shop --image=busybox:1.37 -- sleep 600`
choices.why: A copy keeps the original's spec, variables included, and runs busybox in its place, so it stays up. The broken pod is left alone.

choices.text: `kubectl debug crashing --image=busybox:1.37 --target=shop`
choices.why: An ephemeral container joins a running process, and a pod that crashes on start is gone before anything can attach. It would also stay in the pod's spec for good.

choices.text: `kubectl port-forward pod/crashing 9090:8080`
choices.why: A tunnel needs something listening at the far end, and this process has already exited.

prompt: Under Docker, a small proxy container reached `shelf-web:8080` by name on a network of its own, and `localhost:8080` from inside the proxy was refused. Moved to Kubernetes, the proxy becomes a sidecar in the shop's pod, and its configuration says `localhost:8080`. What happens?
hint: Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 9; Docker and Containers, lesson 23.

choices.text: It is refused, as under Docker, since `localhost` is one container's own loopback
choices.why: That is true of separate containers. A pod wraps its containers in one network namespace, so its loopback is shared.

choices.text: It needs the Service's name, because a pod's containers do not share a loopback
choices.why: The lesson's sidecar fetched the shop's page from `localhost:8080` with no Service in the way.

choices.text: It reaches the shop by the node's address, since each container has one of its own
choices.why: The containers of one pod share one interface and one address, which is why they cannot both listen on the same port.

choices.text: It reaches the shop, because in a pod `localhost` is the pod
choices.why: Both containers share one network namespace, as processes on one small machine do, so the sidecar finds port 8080 without any address.

prompt: A virtual machine carries a role that may only `s3:PutObject` under `example-backups/nightly/*`. The backup container on it was built from an image with `ENV AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE` and the matching secret, left over from a test. The audit log shows the container's calls signed by that key's user and never by the role. What explains it, and what else follows?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 7; Docker and Containers, lesson 18.

choices.text: The environment wins the credential chain, and `ENV` stored the key inside the image
choices.why: The SDK uses the first source that answers, and variables beat the machine's role. And an `ENV` value is stored in the image, so the key has gone wherever the image went.

choices.text: The role's credentials expired after an hour, and the SDK fell back to the next source
choices.why: The provider replaces a role's credentials before they expire. The search stopped at the environment and never reached the role.

choices.text: The trust policy names `ec2.amazonaws.com`, so a container's calls do not get to assume it
choices.why: Nothing was refused: the log shows the calls succeeding as the key's user. Nobody asked for the role.

choices.text: Programs inside containers have no way to the metadata service, so the key was what was left
choices.why: The chain ends with `container-role` and `iam-role` for exactly these programs. A variable earlier in the chain won before either was tried.

prompt: The policy attached to a nightly backup job is up for its quarterly review. Which of these lines are ones lesson 7 says to stop at? Choose all that apply.
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 7.

choices.text: `"Action": "iam:*"`, on an identity whose job is uploading backups
choices.why: An identity that can change IAM can give itself anything. It is administrator access under another name.

choices.text: `"Resource": "*"`
choices.why: A `*` alone in `Resource` puts every bucket in the account in scope, not the one the backups go to.

choices.text: `"Action": "s3:Get*"`, written to mean read-only
choices.why: It also matches `s3:GetBucketPolicy` and every `Get` action S3 adds later. A wildcard in the middle of a name reads narrower than it is.

choices.text: `"Action": "s3:PutObject"` on `arn:aws:s3:::example-backups/nightly/*`
choices.why: One action on one prefix of one bucket is the narrowed policy the lesson writes for this very job.
That is the version of the policy language, the current one, and the value to write.

choices.text: A `StringLike` condition on `s3:prefix` beside `s3:ListBucket`
choices.why: That condition narrows a listing to one prefix. It is the fix for a too-wide `ListBucket`, not a reason for concern.

prompt: An account's API log goes to a bucket in that same account, and the administrators whose calls it records can delete objects there. The reviewers ask for the arrangement lesson 7 describes. What is it, and what does it guard against?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 7; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 3.

choices.text: Record data reads too, so that every `GetObject` on the bucket appears in the log
choices.why: That widens what is recorded. An administrator who can delete the log can still delete those entries with the rest.

choices.text: Turn on versioning in the same bucket, so a deleted entry can be brought back
choices.why: Versioning protects against mistakes, not against somebody allowed to delete versions, and an administrator is allowed.

choices.text: A separate account that only a small security group reaches, with deletion locked until a date
choices.why: Whoever can remove the log can remove the record of what they did. A copy kept by different people, out of their reach, does not share the fate of the account it audits.

choices.text: Keep the account's log for longer than the ninety days the provider holds by default
choices.why: Longer retention answers how far back the log goes, not who can erase it tomorrow.

prompt: An instance's `#cloud-config` user data writes the database password into a file with `write_files`, and the instance boots and works. Who can read that password afterwards?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 4.

choices.text: Nobody after the first boot, because cloud-init deletes the user data once it has run
choices.why: User data runs once; it is not removed. The provider keeps it, and the metadata service still answers with it.

choices.text: Root on the instance alone, since it owns the file that `write_files` created
choices.why: The file is one copy. The user data itself stays readable through the metadata service and through the account.

choices.text: The provider alone, which keeps user data encrypted and does not show it to anybody again
choices.why: Describing the instance shows it to anybody the account allows to do that.

choices.text: Any process on it, through the metadata service, and anyone allowed to describe it
choices.why: User data is not a secret. The way the lesson gives instead is to fetch the password at boot from the provider's secret store, with a role's permissions.

prompt: A public subnet's network ACL admits inbound TCP 443 from `0.0.0.0/0` and lets out TCP 443 to `0.0.0.0/0`, then the `*` deny in each direction. The instance's security group allows 443 in, and the web server listens on `0.0.0.0:443`. From a workstation, `nc -zv -w 3` to the instance's address on port 443 runs. What does it report, and why?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 6; Networks and Protocols, lesson 3.

choices.text: A timeout: the reply goes to the client's ephemeral port, which no outbound rule allows
choices.why: The ACL is stateless, so the reply is judged on its own, and the `*` rule drops it without a word. A dropped packet looks like a dead server, which is why the usual outbound rule covers 1024 to 65535.

choices.text: `Connection refused`, because the ACL rejects the reply on its way out
choices.why: A network ACL drops; it sends nothing back. A refusal would mean the attempt arrived at a port nobody listens on.

choices.text: It connects: the security group is stateful, so the reply leaves on its own
choices.why: The group lets the reply leave the instance. The subnet's ACL is a second filter that remembers nothing, and it still has to allow the reply.

choices.text: It connects, since outbound 443 matches the port the reply comes from
choices.why: Outbound rules match the destination port, and the reply's destination is the client's ephemeral port, not 443.

prompt: A nightly job overwrites `export.csv`, a 2 GB file, in a bucket with versioning on and the lifecycle rule lesson 5 writes, which expires a version 30 days after it stopped being current. Once the rule has been in place for months, about how many GB does that one key hold, counting the current version?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 5.

prompt: A team runs `shelf` on a containers-as-a-service platform. This week's scan of the running image reports a HIGH finding in a package of its base image, and the status has changed to `fixed`. Whose job is it to get the fixed package running?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 1; Docker and Containers, lesson 20.

choices.text: The provider's: it patches the hosts' operating system, which covers the libraries in images
choices.why: The host is the provider's row, and the image is not. A package inside the image changes only when the image is rebuilt.

choices.text: The team's: the base is inside its image, so it rebuilds on the fixed base and redeploys
choices.why: On CaaS the line sits below the runtime: whatever the image carries is the team's to rebuild. Lesson 20's `tzdata` arrives the same way, through a rebuild on a new base.

choices.text: Nobody's until the platform offers the fix in its list of supported runtime versions
choices.why: That is a platform-as-a-service picture, where the runtime is chosen from the provider's list. Here the runtime and its packages travel inside the team's image.

choices.text: The base image's maintainers, whose rebuild reaches the running containers by itself
choices.why: Their rebuild moves a tag in a registry. A running container keeps the bytes it was started from until somebody builds and deploys a new image.

prompt: A shop's cluster runs in two zones of one region, sized so that one zone carries the normal load. Its plan for losing a zone is that pods from the lost zone go `Pending` and the cluster autoscaler adds nodes in the other one. What is that plan relying on, at the worst moment?
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 9; Kubernetes: Orchestration in Production, lesson 34.

choices.text: Nothing beyond the data plane, since adding a node is like serving a request
choices.why: Launching a machine is a control-plane call. The data plane runs what already exists.

choices.text: A second region, since both zones answer to the same regional control systems
choices.why: That is the answer for losing a region. Losing one zone is what two zones are for, if the capacity is already there.

choices.text: The provider launching new machines while many other customers ask for the same
choices.why: Recovering by launching needs the control plane when it is busiest. A statically stable design already runs enough in the other zone, and only the data plane has to move traffic.

choices.text: The pods' real usage, since the autoscaler adds a node when the nodes get busy
choices.why: The cluster autoscaler reacts to pods that cannot be scheduled, by their requests, never by usage.

prompt: A function behind an API opens its own PostgreSQL connection in each execution environment. On a sale day a burst creates 800 environments, and the database refuses connections past its limit. Which of these does lesson 8 offer as answers? Choose all that apply.
hint: Cloud and Serverless, lesson 8.

choices.text: A connection proxy between the functions and the database, lending out a small pool
choices.why: It holds a few real connections and shares them, which environments cannot do among themselves.

choices.text: A concurrency limit on the function, low enough for the database's connection limit
choices.why: Fewer copies at once means fewer connections; requests past the limit are turned away or queued.

choices.text: A database whose interface is HTTP requests rather than long-lived connections
choices.why: With no pool of connections, there is nothing to run out of.

choices.text: More memory for the function, so each environment serves more of the requests
choices.why: More memory buys processor and speed. Each environment still opens its own connection, and the burst still creates hundreds of them.

choices.text: A longer timeout, so a call waits for a free connection instead of failing
choices.why: The database is refusing new connections, not making them wait. And every waiting call holds an environment, and so a connection attempt, for longer.

choices.text: The connection kept in a module-level variable, so the environments share it
choices.why: Module-level code runs once per environment. The variable is shared by the calls of one copy, never across copies.

prompt: The pipeline's history scan finds an AWS access key beginning `AKIA` in the infrastructure repository, added eight months ago and deleted from the files since. The team lead proposes rewriting the history with `git filter-repo` tonight, force-pushing, and rotating the key in the next sprint. What is wrong with the plan?
hint: Cloud Security, lesson 12; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 6.

choices.text: Nothing, provided each developer throws away their clone and clones again after the forced push
choices.why: The clones the team controls are not the problem. Forks, CI caches, backups and every copy made in eight months keep the key, and a rewrite reaches none of them.

choices.text: `git filter-repo` does not reach a commit that old, so the key has to be removed by a new commit instead
choices.why: The rewrite does change every commit, which is why every hash changes. And a new commit removing the line leaves the key in the commits before it.

choices.text: Backwards: the key stops working first, its use is read in the trail, and a rewrite comes last
choices.why: Until the key is worthless, everything else is cosmetic. Its calls since the commit are in the account's records, and rewriting is housekeeping on the copies you hold.

choices.text: Rotation becomes unnecessary once the history is rewritten, since no copy the team holds still has it
choices.why: The copies the team does not hold are the ones that matter, and a leaked key is treated as known to everybody from the push. Only rotating it makes them worthless.

prompt: On 3 December, caio opens a pull request touching the vendor's import bucket, whose policy still carries `#checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_70:vendor import, approved by ana until 2026-11-30, ticket SEC-114`. What does `gate.sh` do with that expired exception, and what would the application pipeline's composition gate have done with an expired line in `ci/exceptions.txt`?
hint: Cloud Security, lesson 14; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 7.

choices.text: `gate.sh` passes, as Checkov never reads the skip's date; the other stage drops that stale line and breaks
choices.why: Checkov does not read the date, so the exception is only as good as whatever looks at it. The composition gate was written to ignore an expired line, so the finding breaks the build again.

choices.text: Both stop the change, because each tool compares the end date written in the exception with the date of today's run
choices.why: Only the composition gate does that, because somebody wrote it to. Checkov treats the comment as a skip and never reads the date inside it.

choices.text: Both let it through: an exception written with a reason and an owner holds until somebody deletes it
choices.why: That is how the skip comment behaves, and it is why lesson 14 wants a reminder or a check of its own. The composition gate refuses a line whose day has passed.

choices.text: `gate.sh` warns instead, since an expired skip turns `CKV_AWS_70` into a warning; the composition gate breaks
choices.why: No such downgrade exists. `--hard-fail-on` names the checks that decide, and the skip removes this one from the run whatever its date says.

prompt: The clinic protects its CloudTrail records in layers. Match each layer to what it stops, as lesson 15 describes it.
hint: Cloud Security, lesson 15.

pairs.left: an explicit `Deny` on `cloudtrail:StopLogging` and its three neighbours
pairs.right: an administrator switching the trail off, despite `AdministratorAccess`

pairs.left: an organisation trail writing into a log-archive account
pairs.right: a production administrator deleting the records from their bucket

pairs.left: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode on that bucket
pairs.right: any user, root included, removing a record before the retention ends
a log file that was edited or never delivered going unnoticed

right_distractors: a stolen key reading the patients' files
a command run inside an instance going unrecorded

prompt: During an incident, the SOC replaced the records database's outbound rule `-1 0.0.0.0/0` with the VPC's range plus the S3 prefix list on port 443. The VPC has had flow logs on, for `ALL` traffic, for months. Lesson 13 never trusted a rule it had not checked. What shows that this one is holding?
hint: Cloud Security, lesson 8; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 13.

choices.text: `describe-security-groups` printing the new egress list, with `0.0.0.0/0` no longer anywhere in it
choices.why: That is the configuration read back. `nft` accepted rules without a complaint too, and a rule with a wrong range reads back just as cleanly.

choices.text: The trail's `RevokeSecurityGroupEgress` record, showing that the call to remove the old rule succeeded
choices.why: A management event says who changed the group and that AWS accepted the change. It says nothing about which packets went where afterwards.

choices.text: A clean run of the posture scanner, which no longer lists the group as open
choices.why: A posture scanner reads configuration through the API, the same thing `describe` reads. It cannot see a single connection.

choices.text: Flow log lines from the database: `REJECT` to outside addresses, `ACCEPT` for the backup to S3
choices.why: Configuration says what is allowed; a flow log says what happened. These are lesson 13's checks: the bad path closed, the good path still open.

prompt: The trail records caio's `PutBucketPolicy` on `clinic-exports` at `2026-10-14T12:02:11Z`. ana's notes, written at the clinic in São Paulo, say she removed the policy at 12:30 that day, local time. Putting both on one clock, as lesson 15 insists, for about how many minutes was the bucket public?
hint: Cloud Security, lesson 15.

prompt: The credential report has a row for dani, who left the clinic in March: no MFA, an active key, last used today. The cloud engineer files it in the posture backlog, to be tidied up in next week's sprint. What is it?
hint: Cloud Security, lesson 6; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 12.

choices.text: A finding: AWS did nothing wrong, so it is a configuration defect, fixed in order of risk
choices.why: That was lesson 6's reading of a permission nobody removed. A key that somebody who left is using today is an incident, not a finding.

choices.text: An incident: declare it, so the record and the clocks start, and stop the key first
choices.why: A working credential in the hands of somebody outside the company is enough, used or not. Declaring early is cheap; declaring late costs evidence and deadlines.

choices.text: A finding until the trail shows the key changed something, since a key that just read files is housekeeping
choices.why: An incident is measured against policy, not damage, and an imminent threat already counts. Reads are often the whole harm.

choices.text: An incident, and the first move is removing dani's policies, so the key is left able to do nothing
choices.why: Close the way in before you tidy the permissions: a key that still works can undo every policy change, which is what dani's key was shown doing.

prompt: During containment, the SOC narrows the records database's outbound rule to `10.20.0.0/16`, and the web servers' queries keep getting their answers. That works because security groups are ___: the reply to a request that was let in goes back out whatever the outbound rules say.
hint: Cloud Security, lesson 8.

prompt: After the exports bucket was public for an afternoon, management asks whether `clinic-records` was read too. The trail's advanced selectors have recorded data events on both buckets since well before that day, and a query for anonymous `GetObject` calls on `clinic-records` returns nothing. How should the incident record state it?
hint: Cloud Security, lesson 15; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 12.

choices.text: As unknown, because a trail's selectors keep who changed a bucket and not who read an object
choices.why: That is true of management events alone. Data events were chosen for both buckets before the incident, so reads of `clinic-records` are recorded.

choices.text: As in scope, since both buckets sit in the same account the stranger could reach
choices.why: Scope follows what the evidence shows was touched. Being reachable in principle puts nothing in scope.

choices.text: As out of scope, citing the records that cover it and the search that found nothing
choices.why: Out of scope is a claim too, and it needs its own evidence: what was checked, and how, so the answer to 'could it be more?' is not a guess.

choices.text: As 'no evidence of access', leaving out what was searched so that the note stays short and readable
choices.why: A negative that does not say what it covered will be read as covering more than it did. The query and the selectors are what make it worth believing.

prompt: The clinic's incident report on the exports bucket reaches its impact section. The trail's data events hold the records lesson 15 read. Which sentence can the report state at the level 'confirmed'?
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 20; Cloud Security, lesson 15.

choices.text: Two files, from 13 and 14 October, went to two outside addresses during the public window
choices.why: The anonymous `GetObject` records show it directly: which files, which addresses, inside the window. That is what confirmed means.

choices.text: The patients in those exports have had their data misused by whoever downloaded the files
choices.why: Nothing in the records says what anybody did with the files. That is not established, and writing it is the alarming direction of a badly written impact.

choices.text: The address that returned after the fix copied the export of 14 October for a second time
choices.why: Its second request, at 15:31:02, carries `errorCode` `AccessDenied`. It was refused, which is the fix holding.

choices.text: No patient was exposed, because S3 had encrypted the exports at rest with its own key
choices.why: Encryption at rest does nothing against a request the service answers: S3 decrypts for anybody it serves. This is the reassuring direction, and it is false.

prompt: The SOC is writing a playbook for the alert 'AWS reports one of our access keys as exposed'. Judged by lesson 5's five questions, which step may the machine take on every alert, with nobody approving it?
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 5; Cloud Security, lesson 7.

choices.text: Delete the exposed key straight away, since a leaked key has to be made worthless as fast as possible
choices.why: Deletion cannot be undone, and a forgotten job may still use the key. It fails the question of reversibility, which is why lesson 7 deactivates and watches first.

choices.text: Deactivate the key, because deactivating is the half of rotation that can be reversed later
choices.why: Reversible, yes, but it stops whatever application holds the key, the way disabling an account stops a person's work. Whether to do it needs judgement.

choices.text: Detach the quarantine policy once a second key exists, so the application keeps running
choices.why: Between deleting the exposed key and detaching the quarantine sits the investigation of what the key did. That is a person's call.

choices.text: Look up the key's owner, its last use and its calls in the trail, and put them in a ticket
choices.why: Enrichment passes all five: it happens often, needs no judgement, changes nothing, touches one key and is well understood. It is what teams automate first.

prompt: The records database's outbound rule was found wide open, and the SOC lists the questions it has to answer. Match each question to the record that answers it.
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 18; Cloud Security, lesson 8.

pairs.left: Did the host talk to `203.0.113.200`, and how many bytes went each way?
pairs.right: a flow log record

pairs.left: What exactly did the host send in that conversation, if it was not encrypted?
pairs.right: a packet capture started before it happened

pairs.left: Who removed the narrow outbound rule from the security group?
pairs.right: a CloudTrail management event

pairs.left: Did an SSH session on the host go on to read the database?
pairs.right: the server's own logs

right_distractors: the security group's rules as they stand now
a CloudTrail data event on the records bucket

prompt: Reading the clinic's trail, the SOC finds dani's refused `StopLogging`, sent from `192.0.2.10`, an address the clinic does not use. Which detection will still fire the next time somebody tries the same thing?
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 9; Cloud Security, lesson 15.

choices.text: A match on `192.0.2.10`, added to the list of known bad addresses the SIEM checks each event against
choices.why: An address sits near the bottom of the pyramid of pain. The next attempt comes from another one, and the list goes stale.

choices.text: An alarm on any `StopLogging`, `DeleteTrail` or `PutEventSelectors`, refused or not
choices.why: It describes the behaviour, not a value, so it survives a new address and a new key. Lesson 15 puts exactly this alarm on the short list that wakes somebody up.

choices.text: An alert on `StopLogging` calls that succeed, since the refused one did no harm to the trail
choices.why: A successful call means the trail is already blind. The refused attempt was the most important line of the afternoon.

choices.text: A watch for dani's key id, `AKIAEXAMPLEDANI00001`, in each new record the trail delivers
choices.why: A single value again, and the key should be deleted anyway. Whoever tries next uses another credential.

prompt: During an incident, ana removed a vendor's bucket policy by hand in the console, and the exposure stopped. The policy is still written in the clinic's Terraform. The next morning, `gate.sh` on `main` ends with a plan that is not empty, though nobody has merged anything. What is the plan saying?
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 14; Cloud Security, lesson 14.

choices.text: That Terraform read the account and will keep ana's change from now on as the new desired state of the bucket
choices.why: Terraform makes the account match the code, not the other way round. The plan is the change needed to put the policy back.

choices.text: Nothing that needs action: the plan just reads, and no apply runs until a reviewer approves it
choices.why: The reviewer is exactly who would reopen the hole, by approving a plan that looks routine. The containment is advice until the code agrees with it.

choices.text: That an apply would bring the policy back: the fix lives only on the account, and has to move into the code
choices.why: The plan is lesson 14's drift check, and it shows the SOC course's trap: rebuild from the old recipe and you rebuild the old hole. Every fix goes into the source.

choices.text: That Checkov has flagged the deleted policy, since a skip comment left with no resource is a finding
choices.why: Checkov reads the files, and the file still holds the policy and its skip. The plan comes from Terraform comparing the code with the account.

prompt: During the incident, `tcpdump` on `fw` has been capturing the records subnet's traffic. The capture is now stopped. Put what happens to the file in the order lesson 18 handles it.
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 18.
items: Stop tcpdump and read how many packets the kernel dropped
Hash the capture file
Write the hash, and who captured it, into the custody record
Make a working copy and check it against the recorded hash
Analyse the copy without root, with display filters
trap: The working copy is not made before the hash is written down: a copy checked against a hash taken afterwards only shows that two copies agree, not that either is what was captured.

prompt: A threat hunt on the clinic's AWS account needs a hypothesis. The trail records management events everywhere, and data events on the two patient buckets only. Which of these can the hunt actually test with that data?
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 10; Cloud Security, lesson 15.

choices.text: If a former contractor's key was used after they left, records carry its `accessKeyId` after their last day
choices.why: Specific, testable with records the account has, and falsifiable: no such records means the hypothesis is false for the period searched.

choices.text: If somebody ran a command on the booking server at night, the trail holds the command itself and who typed it
choices.why: A command inside an instance is not an AWS API call, so no trail records it. That needs the operating system's own logs.

choices.text: If the bucket of public images was read by strangers, the trail's management events show each of those reads
choices.why: A read is a data event, and data events are recorded only for the two patient buckets. Management events hold no reads at all.

choices.text: Somebody may be reading patients' data without the clinic knowing, through a route nobody has found
choices.why: It points at no data and names nothing to look for, so no result could prove it wrong. That is a worry, not a hypothesis.

prompt: The posture scanner flags `clinic-web` as a public bucket every morning. Triage reads it: the rule fired correctly, the bucket really is readable by everybody, and it holds the clinic's website, which is meant to be. From lesson 7's fixed list of closure reasons, it closes as a ___ true positive.
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 7; Cloud Security, lesson 16.

prompt: For a month, the shop's triage feature sent customers' emails to a model provider exactly as they arrived, card numbers and CPFs included. Every reply came back and nothing stopped working. Classified with lesson 12's three impact categories, what does this incident look like?
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 12; AI in Development, lesson 11.

choices.text: Low on each count, since no service stopped and the model refused to use the card numbers
choices.why: A refusal is a reply, and it arrives after the request has already left with everything in it. A silent incident can still be a severe one.

choices.text: No functional impact, a privacy breach, and not recoverable for what has left
choices.why: Nothing broke, personal data went to another company, and a copy outside cannot be called back. The information row is what brings in the lawyer and the DPO today.

choices.text: Not an incident, because a provider under contract is part of the company's own systems
choices.why: Sending data to a provider is handing it to another company, under its terms. And an incident is judged against policy, not against what broke.

choices.text: An integrity loss, since the model was handed data that it was not meant to process
choices.why: Integrity loss is data altered. Here nothing was changed; it was disclosed, which is the privacy breach in the information row.

prompt: The DPO is filling in the ANPD's form for Thursday's incident and asks the SOC for material. Which of these does article 48 of the LGPD list among the contents of the communication? Choose all that apply.
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 21.

choices.text: A description of the nature of the personal data affected
choices.why: First on the list: credentials, contact names and e-mails, and client documents whose content is not yet established.

choices.text: The incident lead's estimate of the fine under article 52
choices.why: Article 52 lists the sanctions the ANPD may apply. Estimating them is nobody's part of the communication.

choices.text: The measures taken to reverse or reduce the effects
choices.why: Lessons 13 and 14 and the actions of lesson 15 supply them.

choices.text: The intruder's address, `203.0.113.66`, for the authority to block
choices.why: The ANPD protects personal data; it blocks nothing. Indicators go to the sharing group, with their marking.

choices.text: The reasons for any delay, if it was not communicated at once
choices.why: On Thursday there are none, if it goes by 22 September.

choices.text: A copy of the exported contacts file, so the authority sees what left
choices.why: That would send the personal data to one more party. The communication describes the data; it does not carry it.

prompt: The clinic's postmortem on the exports bucket reaches its contributing factors. caio wrote the public policy from his laptop, with his own credentials, while the pipeline's gates sat unused beside him. Which finding is written the way lesson 15 asks?
hint: SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 15; Cloud Security, lesson 14.

choices.text: caio went around the pipeline and made the bucket public by hand, from his own laptop
choices.why: It names a person, and a review that ends with a name ends there. The next engineer with the same access can do the same.

choices.text: caio will take the pipeline training again and promise to use it for each future change
choices.why: An action on one person, with nothing a check could confirm. It changes no condition of the system.

choices.text: Human error during a routine change; the team agrees that no further action is needed
choices.why: It names no condition and decides nothing, which is the one outcome a review may not have.

choices.text: People's own credentials could write to the account, so any change could skip every gate in the pipeline
choices.why: A condition that, had it been different, would have stopped the change. It points straight at lesson 14's answer: take write access away from people.

prompt: Lesson 10 prices the support assistant's month, 60,000 requests of 1,500 tokens in and 300 out, at $720 on `claude-opus-5-5`, whose list price is $4 per million tokens in and $20 out. How many of those 720 dollars pay for the output tokens alone?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 10.

prompt: The shop moves its reply drafter onto a Lambda function. The function's execution role holds `AdministratorAccess`, and the drafter offers the model `get_order` and `issue_refund`. A security review asks what bounds the damage when an injected sentence in an email is obeyed. Which change does?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 11; Cloud Security, lesson 13.

choices.text: Offer the drafting task only `get_order`, and narrow the role to what that one tool needs
choices.why: Both are enforced in code, below the model. A tool that is not offered cannot be called, and the role is what any instruction the code obeys inherits.

choices.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt that forbids refunds and any request that mentions secrets
choices.why: It is one more sentence in the same stream as the email. Whether a model obeys it is a matter of probability, and an attacker gets to retry.

choices.text: Move the model provider's API key out of the function's environment into Secrets Manager
choices.why: That protects the key, which is worth doing. The injected instruction still reaches both tools and every permission the role holds.

choices.text: Switch to a larger model, which follows sentences injected into an email less often
choices.why: A defence that works most of the time is one an attacker retries until it does not. It makes the worst case rarer, not smaller.

prompt: Last week a developer committed `.env` with the payment provider's key in it. Today she adds `.env` to `.gitignore`, then asks the editor's assistant why a payment fails, with `.env` open in a tab. What is still true?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 3; Git and Teamwork: Version Control, Review and Process, lesson 10.

choices.text: The new ignore rule keeps `.env` out of the next push, and the key leaves the repository's history with it
choices.why: An ignore rule only applies to files Git is not tracking yet. The file is still tracked, and last week's commit keeps the key whatever happens next.

choices.text: The assistant skips the files git ignores, so the repository is the one thing left to worry about
choices.why: The editor does not care what git ignores: an ignored file is still a file on disk. Keeping it from the assistant takes an exclusion list of its own.

choices.text: Git still tracks the file, last week's commit keeps the key, and the open tab reaches the assistant
choices.why: Each layer needs its own answer: `git rm --cached` to stop tracking, an exclusion for the assistant, and above all a new key, because the old one has left.

choices.text: `git rm --cached .env` takes the key out of last week's commit, as well as out of the next commit made
choices.why: It removes the file from the staging area and records its removal from now on. Earlier commits keep it, which is why the key has to be revoked.

prompt: An agent built on lesson 7's host is going into production. Which of its limits sit below the model, where nothing the model writes can change them? Choose all that apply.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 7.

choices.text: `MAX_STEPS`, enforced by the host's own loop
choices.why: A `for` loop stops when it stops, whatever the model asks for next.

choices.text: The `--rules` system prompt saying each fact needs a tool result
choices.why: It made invention rarer in the lesson's runs; it did not make an answer checked. The model reads it in the same stream as everything else.

choices.text: The refusal of a second call with the same tool and arguments
choices.why: The host checks the call before running it, so a model stuck in a loop is stopped at the repeat.

choices.text: A downloaded server marking each of its tools `readOnlyHint`
choices.why: That is the server's own description of itself, a hint a host should not rely on unless it trusts the server.

choices.text: `read_handbook` resolving a path before comparing it with the folder
choices.why: The check is in the tool and is about what the argument resolves to, so `../../.env` is refused whoever asked.

choices.text: A tool description telling the model when it may use the tool
choices.why: A description is text the model reads and may follow. It says when to use a tool; it enforces nothing.

prompt: A reply drafter refunded an order in full because of a sentence inside a customer's email. Put the response in the order lesson 11 gives it.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 11.
items: Stop the damage: flip the off switch, or remove the tool that paid
Revoke whatever may have leaked: a key, a token, a session
Undo what can be undone: reverse the refund and tell the customer
Fix the cause in the host: the tool offered, the check, the approval
Add this email to the evaluation, so the next model meets it too
trap: Fixing the cause does not come first: while the tool is still offered, the next email with the same sentence pays again, so the damage is stopped before anybody improves the host.

prompt: A failed job printed its environment while somebody was debugging it, and the CI log now shows the shop's `OPENAI_API_KEY`. The log is readable by everybody with access to the project's builds. What comes first?
hint: AI in Development, lesson 10; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 6.

choices.text: Delete the log; the project is private, so just colleagues could have read the key
choices.why: Private is a list of people, and it changes. A CI log is often kept longer than the code, and deleting it now recalls no copy already made.

choices.text: Revoke the key now and put a new one where the job reads it, without waiting for any proof of misuse
choices.why: Revoke on suspicion, not on proof. A new key costs a deploy; an old key in the wrong hands costs whatever its limit allows.

choices.text: Check the provider's usage page, and revoke it if it shows spending nobody can explain
choices.why: That waits for proof, and the proof arrives as a bill. By then the key has been working for whoever holds it.

choices.text: Put a spending limit on the key, so that a leak costs a bounded amount, and keep using it
choices.why: A limit bounds the bill and is worth having anyway. The key still works for anybody who read the log.

prompt: The pipeline gains an AI review bot beside its tests, its linter and a secret scan. Which of these may decide, on their own, whether a pull request merges? Choose all that apply.
hint: AI in Development, lesson 4; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 7.

choices.text: A test that fails
choices.why: A test is true or false, which is what a check gating a merge has to be.

choices.text: The bot's approval of the whole change
choices.why: Never the decision to merge: a bot's approval is a claim, and lesson 4's review made three confident claims and missed the real bug.

choices.text: A secret found by the scan
choices.why: A secret always breaks the build: its owner can act at once, by revoking it.

choices.text: A linter error on a line the change added
choices.why: Like the tests and the type checker, a linter's answer is true or false.

choices.text: A bot comment calling one function a serious problem
choices.why: A finding is a hypothesis to check by reading the line or writing a test. It informs the person who decides.

choices.text: More than five bot comments on one pull request
choices.why: A count of claims is still claims. Gating on it would break builds on findings nobody has checked, and the gate would be switched off.

prompt: The composition-analysis stage of your DevSecOps portfolio project reports an advisory against a package you depend on, and the advisory names no fixed version. You want the repository to show what a reviewer in your track looks for. What do you do with this finding?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 3; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 7.

choices.text: Break the build until the package's maintainers publish a fix, so the README shows a gate taken seriously
choices.why: Nobody pushing to your project can publish somebody else's release, so every push stops on a finding no change can fix. That is the gate that gets switched off within weeks.

choices.text: Let it warn, and record who read the notice and whether your code reaches the affected part
choices.why: With no version to move to, the gate warns and a named person reads the advisory, as with ecdsa, where signing was affected and verification was not. A finding accepted with a written reason is exactly the triage a DevSecOps reviewer opens the pipeline to find.

choices.text: Put it in the exceptions file with no end date, so the pipeline stops mentioning it and the README stays clean
choices.why: An exception carries a date, a reason and an owner, and it expires. One with no date is a baseline by another name: a decision nobody looks at again.

choices.text: Take the composition stage out of the pipeline until a fixed version exists, and say so in the README
choices.why: A stage that is not run is the line that turns a gate into a decoration, however honestly it is announced. The reviewer came to see a finding handled, not a scanner removed.

prompt: Your portfolio project runs its tests with the workflow lesson 12 of the portfolio course shows: `on: [push, pull_request]`, then `actions/checkout@v4` and one more action named by its `@v5` tag, with no `permissions` key. A DevSecOps reviewer reads it against the controls the supply-chain course applies to a workflow file. Which changes would those controls ask for? Choose all that apply.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 12; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 16.

choices.text: Name each action by a full commit hash, with its version in a comment beside it
choices.why: A tag can be moved by whoever controls the action's repository, which is what happened to tj-actions/changed-files; a commit hash cannot. The comment tells the next reader which release the hash stands for.

choices.text: Name each action by its exact release tag, such as `v4.2.2`, instead of the major one
choices.why: A precise tag is still a tag, and a tag can be moved to another commit. The moved tags in the tj-actions incident were version tags too.

choices.text: Declare `permissions: contents: read` in the file, for every job
choices.why: When the file says nothing, the repository's or organisation's default applies, and a setting can be changed by an administrator with no trace in a review. A line in the workflow is reviewed with the code.

choices.text: Add `persist-credentials: false` to the checkout step
choices.why: By default `actions/checkout` writes the job's token into `.git/config`, where later steps and anything that uploads the workspace can read it. This keeps it out.

choices.text: Trigger on `pull_request_target`, so that a fork's pull request also gets the tests run with the secrets
choices.why: That trigger runs in the context of the base repository, with a token that can write and its secrets, even for a fork. It exists for jobs that never run the pull request's code; `pull_request` runs a fork's code with a read-only token and no secrets, which is what tests need.

prompt: Your portfolio repository is public. You pushed a commit holding `SMTP_PASSWORD = "..."`, deleted the file in the next commit, and pushed again. Two hours later a friend says: rewrite the history with `git filter-repo`, force-push, and it is as if it never happened. If you do only that, what is left?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 14; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 6.

choices.text: Little that matters: the force-push replaces the branch, and the hosting site drops the old commits from every fork
choices.why: Forks are copies under somebody else's account and are not touched by your push. The hosting site's own documentation says cached views and pull-request references can keep the old commits reachable too.

choices.text: A stray copy in your laptop's reflog, which git clears away by itself within a few weeks
choices.why: That reasoning fits a branch nobody pushed, which is what lesson 14 threw away. Once pushed, every clone made in those two hours holds the commit as well.

choices.text: No finding a scanner would report, since the password was gone from the tip of the pushed branch
choices.why: Secret scanners read history, not only the latest files: `gitleaks git` reads what every commit added. Scanners of public repositories find a key within minutes of the push.

choices.text: A password that still works, sitting in every copy made before the force-push
choices.why: A rewrite changes your copy and no other. What makes the copies harmless is revoking the password at the mail provider, which comes first; cleaning the history is optional and comes last.

prompt: Your project deploys the way loanbook does: the Containerfile copies the code in and ends with `USER 1000`, and the Quadlet file mounts `loanbook-data:/data:U`. The README claims that nothing running in the container can change the application's code. What does the supply-chain course's lesson on safe execution say is wrong with that claim?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 15; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 9.

choices.text: It rests on the user alone: whoever starts the container can choose user 0, and only a read-only root then holds
choices.why: `USER` is the user a container starts as when nothing says otherwise. One `--user 0` makes the process root and it rewrites `app.py`; with the root read-only, the same write fails.

choices.text: Podman ignores `USER` in a Quadlet unit, so every container started that way runs as root anyway
choices.why: Nothing in either lesson says so. The image's user applies unless whoever starts the container overrides it, and that override is the actual gap.

choices.text: The `:U` on the volume hands the code under `/app` to user 1000 as well, so the application can rewrite its own files
choices.why: `:U` changes the owner of the volume mounted at `/data`, nothing else. The code under `/app` was copied in by root and stays root's.

choices.text: Nothing is wrong: a process that is not root has no way at all to gain root inside a container
choices.why: `NoNewPrivs: 0` means running a setuid program can still raise privileges, and the container keeps capabilities within reach for anything that does. That is why the lesson goes on to take them away.

prompt: You review your own branch `empty-state` before opening its pull request, the way lesson 10 reviews loanbook's. Put the steps in the order the lesson takes them.
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 10.
items: `git diff --stat main...empty-state`, to see whether the change is small enough to read in one sitting
`git diff main...empty-state`, read top to bottom as if somebody else had written it
a `grep -nE` over the lines the branch adds, which finds a `console.log` and a `TODO`
`git commit -q -a --fixup HEAD`, then a rebase with `--autosquash` onto `main`, folding the cleanup into the one commit
a description whose last part names the older injection problem and the card opened for it
trap: The fixup cannot come before the search, because there is nothing to fold in until the two slips have been found. And the injection problem is not fixed on this branch at all: it predates the change, so it ends in the description with a card of its own.

prompt: Your pre-commit hook has to look at what is about to be committed rather than at the working tree, and only at the lines being added. Complete its first command as lesson 14 writes it: `git diff --___ -U0 | grep -inE '^\+.*(password|secret|token|api_?key)...'`
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 14.

prompt: loanbook's stylesheet turns the table into cards with `@media (max-width: 36rem)`, which lesson 13 puts at about 576 pixels at the default font size. A teacher who reads with a larger font has set her browser's default font size to 20 pixels. Below what window width, in pixels, does she get the card layout?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 13.

prompt: In an interview for a DevSecOps role, the interviewer reads out a decision from your README: *No accounts. The borrower is a name typed in.* and, further on, *The cost is that anybody who can open the page can lend.* Then she asks: is that a risk you have accepted? What is the honest answer, by the threat-modelling course?
hint: The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 16; Threat Modelling and Risk, lesson 12.

choices.text: Yes: a decision written down beside its cost is what accepting a risk means
choices.why: Writing the cost down is a good start, and it is not yet an acceptance. Without an owner and a date, it is a risk somebody hopes will go away.

choices.text: No: an accepted risk has to be reduced before it can be accepted, and a name typed into a form reduces nothing
choices.why: Accepting a risk is a legitimate decision in its own right, taken when the controls cost more than they save. Nothing has to be mitigated before it.

choices.text: Not yet: it says what was decided and why, but names nobody who accepted it, and no date to look again
choices.why: A legitimate acceptance is made by the right person, in writing, knowing what they accept, for a limited time. The README has the reasoning; who accepted it, by name, and when it will be reviewed are missing.

choices.text: Not yet: it lacks a DREAD score for the threat, which is what an acceptance is signed against
choices.why: The record the lesson asks for is the risk with its estimate, why, what is in place instead, who and when. It names no scoring scheme, and DREAD is one method among several.

prompt: Six weeks into your first job, your change to the login service's configuration takes sign-in down for forty minutes. You said so in the team's channel within minutes and helped roll it back. The postmortem draft lists, as a contributing factor: *the new engineer pushed a broken configuration*. What should that line become?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 15.

choices.text: It should stay as it is, because owning a mistake means having your name written in the record beside it
choices.why: You owned it where it counted, by saying so early and helping fix it. A factor that names a person leads to an action about that person and leaves the system as it was.

choices.text: *Human error during a configuration change*, which keeps the fact and names nobody
choices.why: It names nobody and still describes a person rather than a condition. Nothing in it says what a change could fix, so no action can come from it.

choices.text: It should come out of the postmortem altogether, since an honest slip by a junior belongs in the one-to-one
choices.why: Your manager may well hear about it there, and the review still needs it: the conditions that let one change take sign-in down are still in place.

choices.text: A condition of the system: a configuration change could reach production with nothing checking sign-in
choices.why: A blameless review asks what let a reasonable action cause harm, and writes it as a contributing factor a change can remove. Your own part is the sentence on what you will do differently.

prompt: In your first month you join the on-call rota. At night an alert fires, and the runbook's command to isolate the server fails: the interface it names was renamed. A senior answers your message with the command that works, and the alert is handled. What do you do the next morning?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 20; SOC, Monitoring and Incident Response, lesson 11.

choices.text: Keep the working command in your own notes, so that you never need to ask that question again
choices.why: Writing the answer down is right; your notebook is the wrong place for it. The next person on the rota meets the same broken step at night, with the same runbook in front of them.

choices.text: Put the working step into the runbook and run it once, so the next person on the rota finds a procedure that works
choices.why: A runbook is only good if it has been run, and it has to be tested again when the system changes. Turning your own question into a page for the next person is what a team values in a junior.

choices.text: Leave the runbook to its owner: in the first ninety days a junior asks, and does not change procedures
choices.why: Nothing in the first ninety days says to wait; the questions you asked are meant to become notes for the next person. Left alone, the broken step fails again on somebody else's night.

choices.text: Ask the same senior again the next time it fires, since asking is part of a junior's job
choices.why: Asking is part of the job, and so is asking each thing once. The answer has to be written where it will be found.

prompt: In a junior DevSecOps interview you are told: *a clinic's portal is getting a feature where patients upload the PDFs of their exams. How would you threat model it?* What do you do first?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 14; Threat Modelling and Risk, lesson 1.

choices.text: Ask what must never happen, then draw its parts, the data between them and where trust changes
choices.why: Clarifying comes before anything is drawn, and the drawing answers the first of the four questions: what are we working on. Every threat named afterwards is tied to a part of it.

choices.text: Go through the STRIDE categories one by one and give a threat for each, which shows the method is known
choices.why: A list made without a drawing of this system fits every system equally badly. The interviewer is checking whether you ask before you build.

choices.text: Say you would run static and dynamic scanners over the upload code first, and model whatever they find
choices.why: The feature is not built yet, and scanners walk past a flaw in the design anyway: a missing step leaves no line to flag.

choices.text: Propose a penetration test of the upload first, since it gives evidence about the system instead of guesses
choices.why: A pentest attacks a built system and tests the implementation after the fact. A threat model reasons about the design, and tells a pentester where to look later.

prompt: Your DevSecOps portfolio project is a small service whose pipeline scans for secrets, static-analysis findings and vulnerable dependencies, and whose README walks through one finding from the scan to its fix. Which line describes it on your CV?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 4; The Portfolio Project: From Brief to Deploy, lesson 3.

choices.text: Configured gitleaks, Semgrep, Bandit and pip-audit in a GitHub Actions pipeline
choices.why: A list of tools describes a project that works and one that never ran equally well. It says what you used, and the reader wanted what you did.

choices.text: Reduced the project's known vulnerabilities by 85% after adding automated security scanning to every push
choices.why: Measured how, against what? A number nobody can explain turns the interview into a check on your honesty, and a project's own scan has no honest baseline for it.

choices.text: Built CI that refuses a pushed credential, and documented one issue from detection to repair
choices.why: What you did, what is now true, and evidence anybody can check: the pattern of a project line. It is also what a DevSecOps reviewer opens first, a security gate and a finding handled end to end.

choices.text: Was responsible for the security of a CI/CD pipeline in a personal web project
choices.why: *Was responsible for* is one of the openings that hide what you did. It names no result and nothing to check.

prompt: A take-home for a junior DevSecOps role: *add security checks to this repository's pipeline*, about three hours suggested. On the first run, static analysis reports forty findings, all in code written long before you arrived. When the three hours are up, what do you hand in? Choose all that apply.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 13; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 7.

choices.text: A note saying the gate breaks only on findings that are new since a recorded baseline, and why
choices.why: Separating new findings from the ones that were there before is the way out of a first run full of old ones, and the note is where what you chose, and why, belongs.

choices.text: The forty, under what you would do with more time, as a list to triage
choices.why: A baseline is a starting point with a plan attached, and the note's last part is where the missing pieces go.

choices.text: All forty set to break the build, since a warning is a gate nobody reads
choices.why: A gate that breaks on findings the person pushing did not add stops the team on day one and is switched off by day three.

choices.text: `continue-on-error: true` on the scanning step, so that the reviewer opens a green pipeline
choices.why: That line is how a gate becomes a decoration, and a reviewer of a DevSecOps take-home is looking for exactly that.

choices.text: What you have when the time is up, rather than forty fixes made over the weekend
choices.why: The reviewer compares the work with what is reasonable in the suggested time, and is also checking how you behave with a deadline.

choices.text: Forty fixes, one commit each, since the brief asked for checks that pass
choices.why: A submission that obviously took four evenings says you did not read the brief or cannot estimate. Stop when the time runs out and say what is missing.

prompt: Three months into a job search for DevSecOps roles, your tracker shows these rejections. Match each one to how lesson 19 reads it.
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 19.

pairs.left: a no right after the screening call
pairs.right: most often a practical mismatch: salary, contract, shift or location

pairs.left: a single no after a technical interview
pairs.right: the exercise, the thinking aloud, or simply a stronger candidate that day

pairs.left: the fifth no at the same technical stage
pairs.right: a leaking stage, fixed by practising out loud with a person watching

pairs.left: a no after the final interview
pairs.right: usually close: somebody else fitted slightly better

right_distractors: evidence that you are not good enough for the field
a CV and an aim to fix before anything else

prompt: In a live exercise the interviewer asks whether a secret was ever committed to a small repository. You run `gitleaks dir` over it, the scan ends with `no leaks found`, and you suspect that is not the whole answer but cannot remember the rest. What do you do?
hint: From Study to Hired: CV, Interviews and the First 90 Days, lesson 12; Pipeline and Supply Chain Security, lesson 6.

choices.text: Say that the repository is clean: the exit status is the scanner's verdict, and it was 0
choices.why: The verdict covers only what was scanned. `gitleaks dir` reads the files as they are now, and the question was about every commit.

choices.text: Say where you are: that read the files as they are now, and the question was about history
choices.why: Saying where you are stuck tells the interviewer exactly what help is useful, and the missing piece is `gitleaks git`, which reads what every commit added.

choices.text: Go quiet and read through the tool's help until you find the option that reads the whole history
choices.why: From the outside, silence looks the same as having no idea. Say what you are looking for, then look.

choices.text: Guess at a flag that might cover the history, and keep trying variations until the tool accepts one
choices.why: Pretending to know an interface is what the lesson says not to do. Say what you would look up, and carry on.
